content: 1. The Guideline Development Group (GDG) identified sexually transmitted infection (STI) conditions that were not included in the 2003 WHO STI guidelines but were deemed important and common enough to be reviewed and added to the updated WHO STI guidelines. 2. Certain STI conditions included in the 2003 WHO STI guidelines were not updated but were selected by the GDG to remain in the new guidelines. These conditions are rare, and their diagnosis is infrequent in most settings. Additionally, there is limited new information available to justify changes to the 2003 recommendations. 3. Some STI conditions not included in the 2003 WHO STI guidelines but present in other national guidelines were not selected by the GDG for inclusion in the updated WHO STI guidelines. 4. In December 2013, the GDG convened to discuss and finalize an initial list of population, intervention, comparator, and outcome (PICO) questions identified by WHO. These questions were used to guide the development of the updated guidelines. 5. Surveys were conducted among GDG subgroups with expertise in specific STIs (e.g., gonorrhea, chlamydia, syphilis, herpes simplex virus type 2). The purpose of these surveys was to rank the importance of populations, interventions, and outcomes for each STI condition on a scale of 1 to 9. Rankings of 7–9 were considered critical, 4–6 were important, and 1–3 were not important. 6. Four priority STI surveys achieved a 90–100% response rate from GDG subgroup members. The results were analyzed, and only critical interventions were compared with each other and with important interventions. Important interventions were not compared to each other. 7. Based on feedback, a revised list of priority questions was compiled, and all GDG members reviewed them. Six priority questions were identified for updating gonorrhea treatment recommendations, each framed using the PICO format. 8. For uncomplicated genital and anorectal gonococcal infections in adults, adolescents, HIV-positive patients, and men who have sex with men (MSM), recommended treatments include ceftriaxone (≥250 mg intramuscularly, single dose) or alternative regimens such as cefixime, azithromycin, gentamicin, spectinomycin, or kanamycin. Dual therapy options were also evaluated. 9. For pregnant women with uncomplicated genital and anorectal gonococcal infections, similar treatment regimens were recommended, with additional considerations for fetal and maternal outcomes, including toxicity, teratogenicity, and STI transmission risks. 10. For gonococcal oropharyngeal infections in adults and adolescents, treatment options included ceftriaxone (≥250 mg intramuscularly, single dose) or alternative regimens such as cefixime, azithromycin, or gentamicin. Dual therapy options were also assessed. 11. For cases of treatment failure of gonorrhea to cephalosporins, alternative regimens included combinations of gentamicin, spectinomycin, gemifloxacin, or azithromycin. Critical outcomes included microbiological cure, compliance, and prevention of complications. 12. For ophthalmia neonatorum in neonates, treatment and prevention strategies were reviewed, focusing on the absence of complications such as conjunctivitis, keratitis, blindness, and corneal scarring. 13. Evidence for the effects of interventions was searched using a hierarchical approach to avoid duplication of previously published reviews. This included identifying pre-existing synthesized evidence from systematic reviews and conducting new systematic reviews when necessary. 14. Search strategies were developed by an information specialist and included keywords based on PICO questions. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) were prioritized for critical and important outcomes, while non-randomized studies were included when RCT evidence was unavailable. 15. Data extraction was performed independently by two researchers using a pilot-tested form. Disagreements were resolved through discussion with a third team member. Data included patient characteristics, diagnosis, treatment regimens, settings, follow-up, and outcomes. 16. Meta-analyses were conducted using pooled results from RCTs and non-randomized studies. Heterogeneity was explored, and absolute effects were calculated using relative effects and baseline risks agreed upon by the GDG. 17. Studies on patient values, preferences, acceptability, equity, and feasibility were identified through systematic searches. These studies included qualitative research, patient utility assessments, and non-utility measurements of health states. 18. Cost analyses were conducted to estimate the direct costs of medications for each treatment option. These estimates included the market price of medicines and procurement costs but excluded other resource costs such as syringes or injection time. 19. The final cost per full course of treatment was calculated based on the number of doses per day, treatment duration, and procurement costs. Unit prices were obtained from the 2014 MSH/WHO International Drug Price Indicator Guide.
